title: Rule of Law
text:
During Donald Trump’s presidential campaign, he often talked about going after the “worst of the worst” in immigration enforcement. That was never going to be the case, because illegal immigrants simply do not commit violent crime at the rate that Trump has claimed. We are now seeing that reflected in the data, with the vast majority of deportees or detainees having little-to-no criminal record.
In early October, ICE agents raided a Chicago apartment building in the middle of the night, with agents breaking down doors and a helicopter hovering overhead. The justification for the raid was that the building was “filled with TdA terrorists,” according to White House homeland security advisor Stephen Miller. A Pro Publica investigation identified 21 of the 37 immigrants detained in the raid (federal officials declined to release the list). The investigation found that no criminal charges have been filed against anyone in the raid, and no criminal convictions at all for 18 of the 21 individuals. Federal officials have not provided evidence of Tren de Aragua membership for the two individuals they claim were in the gang. To sum up, families were detained in the middle of the night, had children taken detained in their pajamas, and had their apartments ransacked, all so the Trump administration could press zero charges. But at least they got a neat video of agents repelling from helicopters and breaking doors down.
On a broader scale, CBS News looked into over 600 individuals detained by ICE in the Chicago area. Just 16 of them had criminal histories that merited “high risk” designations by the federal government.

title: Rule of Law
text:
Selective Enforcement
The Trump administration has upended the Department of Justice, choosing not to enforce laws against favored parties, while demanding investigations that result in any type of conviction against disfavored parties.
The New York Times interviewed 60+ DOJ officials who have been fired or resigned to get their stories. Some of the highlights include Trump administration officials:

Stopping enforcement of laws that prevent companies giving bribes in foreign countries and transparency requirements for people working for foreign countries.
Demanding charges be brought against universities, rather than allowing an investigation to determine whether charges are justified.
Ordering FBI field offices to spend at least 1/3 of their time on immigration enforcement, removing resources from ongoing investigations of violent crime, drug trafficking, and child exploitation.
Demanding charges be brought against James Comey, and firing or forcing resignation from prosecutors who said that there was not sufficient evidence. (The Comey case has now hit a rough patch because the prosecutor put in place of those fired/resigned officials is now being cited for prosecutorial misconduct.)

An important quote from one of the officials in the story: “I really fear the Justice Department — which has a good record of convicting dangerous, violent people — won’t see the same success rate, because people will think it’s not on the level.”
The focus on illegal immigration has also taken away law enforcement focus from other priorities. According to government documents, Department of Homeland Security officials spent 33% fewer hours on child exploitation cases from February through April compared to previous years. Other teams that have been diverted to illegal immigration assignments include those working on tracking black market oil from Iran, antiterrorism intelligence, training of federal law enforcement (including the Secret Service), and human trafficking. (Source)

title: Rule of Law
text:
Corruption
US tariffs on Switzerland were reduced from 39% to 15% this week. There isn’t anything wrong with reducing tariffs, typically. However, in this case, tariffs were only reduced after a Swiss delegation visited the White House and gifted President Trump an engraved gold bar and a Rolex desk clock (Source). It is yet another example of the transactional nature of this presidency–that President Trump will often only provides benefits for a country or company if he personally has gotten something out of the deal.
The Department of Homeland Security has spent more than $200 million on an ad campaign intended to discourage illegal immigration. ProPublica found that the largest recipient of those contracts is one with significant ties to Department of Homeland Security officials. The subcontractor’s CEO is the husband of the DHS chief spokesperson, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem has previously used the Ohio-based firm for her own gubernatorial campaigns and other South Dakota projects, and Noem adviser Corey Lewandowski has previously worked with the firm. DHS has claimed that they had no involvement in the selection. However, the declared “national emergency” at the border meant that normal competitive bidding processes were bypassed, so there is little transparency in the process short of a Congressional inquiry.

title: Facebook: October 10th
text:
The following text is from a Facebook post made on October 10th, 2025. (Original Post)
It’s been a bit since I’ve posted about politics, but that doesn’t mean things have gotten better. On Tuesday, President Trump told all of the top U.S. generals and admirals that U.S. cities should be “training grounds” for the military. That is increasingly proven out, as more and more U.S. citizens and other legal immigrants get caught up in immigration raids. At the same time, President Trump has recently fired U.S. attorneys who disagreed about the evidence for prosecuting his political enemies, and has unilaterally made deals with countries that have supported his personal projects. All of these are disturbing steps in an authoritarian direction.
A couple of days ago, U.S. federal agents stormed into an apartment building, breaking into nearly every unit and zip-tying residents, including U.S. citizens, to keep them outside until the raid was completed. The raid included tearing through apartments and destroying personal property, all while never showing the residents a warrant or allowing access to lawyers. (Source)
An elderly owner of a car wash in California has filed a lawsuit after being body slammed and injured by federal agents during an immigration raid. When agents arrived, he came out to offer proof of his employees’ legal authorizations, but instead was taken to the ground. (Source)
Multiple class action lawsuits have been placed against ICE for indiscriminate arrests and detainments, including against U.S. citizens. In one, the lead plaintiff says he was taken off the street by agents who did not ask about his immigration status. When he tried to tell them that he had valid immigration papers, he was told, “No you don’t. You are illegal.” and “Shut up, bitch, you’re illegal.” He was detained overnight until an ICE supervisor realized the next morning that he did, in fact, have a valid immigration status. (Source 1, Source 2)
In another class action suit, the lead plaintiff is an Alabama man who was detained two different times by immigration agents, despite showing the agents his REAL ID driver’s license. (Source)
The Department of Homeland Security has claimed that in some of these cases, the individuals were obstructing officers or assaulted officers, with those being the reasons for their detainment or arrest. However, in most of these cases there have not been charges filed by federal authorities or any charges filed have been dropped, nor has DHS provided evidence of assault on the officers. (Department of Homeland Security, Source Describing Dropped Charges)
These raids come from ICE and other law enforcement officers at local and federal levels who have been assigned to this work. The libertarian CATO Institute identified that over 25,000 local and federal officers were diverted from their normal jobs to instead focus on immigration enforcement. Correspondingly, CATO has documented decreased criminal referrals from some of these agencies as a result, such as the Drug Enforcement Administration. That is, law enforcement being taken away from their normal jobs investigating and prosecuting crime to instead arrest or detain people who are largely productive members of society who have not committed crimes. (Source)
A U.S. attorney was fired after she reminded a Border Patrol chief to follow a court order that prevented arrests without probable cause. This comes along with a firing or forced resignation of another U.S. attorney after he maintained that there was not sufficient evidence to bring charges against President Trump’s enemies. Other attorneys in the same office have been fired for similar political reasons following calls from social media influencers. (Source 1, Source 2, Source 3)
The Trump administration “Immigration Czar,” Tom Homan, is a source of especially high controversy right now. In an undercover FBI operation last year, he accepted $50,000, in return promising government contracts after joining the Trump administration. The Justice Department dropped the investigation after President Trump’s inauguration. At the same time, Bloomberg reported that Homan is still involved in immigration detention contracting, despite some of the companies being his former clients. (Source 1, Source 2, Source 3)
Moving beyond immigration, President Trump recently signed an executive order promising to defend Qatar upon any attack. This was not approved by Congress. It also comes after Qatar gifted a plane to the U.S. that Trump intends to use for Air Force One and maintain for personal use after his presidency, as well as Trump organization plans for a golf resort in Qatar, supported by the country’s sovereign wealth fund. Notably, Trump has criticized similar security guarantees for NATO countries, but chose to unilaterally create this guarantee. (Source)
The U.S. also recently made advanced computer chips available for purchase and use in the United Arab Emirates. This deal came disturbingly close to a deal made by the same U.A.E. royal to invest $2 billion in cryptocurrency from World Liberty Financial–the crypto company owned by the Trump and Witkoff families. Notably, Steve Witkoff (of that Witkoff family) is also the special envoy to the Middle East, simultaneously negotiating with the U.A.E. on the chips deal while also having a financial interest in the company that benefitted from U.A.E. investment (Steve Witkoff is not fully divested yet, and his son Zach is also a leader of World Liberty Financial). (Source)
Earlier this summer, I also meant to post something about the Trump administration’s interference with private businesses, but never got around to it. Under a Democratic administration, all of the deals below would no doubt be labeled as socialist or communist.
The U.S. now owns a “golden share” of U.S. Steel after the Nippon Steel acquisition of the company in June. Under this deal, the U.S. government has significant decision-making authority over the company. (Source)
Intel gave the U.S. government a 10% stake in the company. This came after President Trump had called for Intel’s CEO to resign. After the deal, Trump described the CEO as a “success.” (Source)
Shortly before the Intel deal, Trump announced that Nvidia would be giving the U.S. 15% of the revenue it gets from computer chip sales in China. It appears that this deal was required for the administration to give Nvidia the ability to sell the chips in China. (Source)
This should be needless to say, but it is a bad thing when businesses feel they have to provide personal benefits to a political leader in order to avoid unfavorable treatment.

title: Facebook: April 25th
text:
The following text is from a Facebook post made on April 25th, 2025. (Original Post)
I wanted to follow-up from my post several weeks ago concerning the Trump administration’s slide towards authoritarianism. There is so much news that no individual can really keep up, and neither can the justice system.
Those who have experienced other countries’ moves towards authoritarianism describe this as the way it happens–a pace that is so fast that citizens have little ability to react until it is too late, while the leader uses the pace to help normalize ideas that would be unfathomable except in this context.
This article talks about some of those other countries’ examples and highlights that in an authoritarian slide there is no moment like the present to take action.
A Ticking Clock on American Freedom
Again, the articles below aren’t about my disagreements with President Trump and the administration on policy, but instead are about my concerns for the lack of separation of powers, due process, humanity, and integrity.
President Trump has talked multiple times about sending U.S. citizens to the same prison in El Salvador where others have been sent without due process. Remember that the administration has claimed that once someone is there, they have no way to return them to the U.S. or even request their return. That means that any person, citizen or not, guilty or not, is essentially sent there for life. (Source)
Quite a few U.S. citizens have incorrectly received emails telling them they needed to leave the country immediately, at the very least continuing to show an indifference by the Trump administration towards getting things correct. Wisconsin Public Radio, NBC News, ABC10 News San Diego, WIRED
A 60 Minutes investigation into the (at the time) 238 people sent to the El Salvador prison found that only a dozen or so had committed violent crimes. About 20% had committed non-violent offenses. A whopping 75% did not have a criminal record in the U.S. or abroad. (Source)
A U.S. citizen was detained by ICE under a law that already is suspended, and was only released several hours after his mother showed his birth certificate to a judge. (Source)
Another U.S. citizen was detained for 10 days. DHS has claimed that he had told ICE agents that he was in the country illegally, though their official story has changed over several official filings. The individual insists that he said he was a citizen. Nonetheless, he was still held for some time after his family brought documentation for his citizenship. (Source)
Yet another U.S. citizen was detained for nearly five hours after returning from a Palm Sunday celebration in Canada. (Source)
The Trump administration ended refugee programs for refugees from Afghanistan. Many of them, such as Afghan Christians, will have nowhere to go other than back to Afghanistan, where they are likely to face significant persecution. New York Times, Christian Post
An Australian man with a valid visa who had been living and working in the U.S. for 5+ years was detained and then deported after returning to the U.S. following his sister’s funeral. (Source)
Iowa State has had at least one student’s visa revoked, as well as an alum’s. The alum was presumably flagged because he was once charged with evading arrest. But an investigation found that he did so unknowingly and the charge was dropped. (Source)
Broadly, the Trump administration appears to be using any speech they disagree with or any violations, no matter how minor, as reasons to revoke student visas, then give minimal or no warning to the students before the deadline by which they are supposed to have “self-deported.” (Source 1, Source 2)
The administration moved a man from Pennsylvania to Texas against a judge’s order. (Source)
A man’s family learned after more than a month that he had been taken to El Salvador. They learned this from NBC News rather than any federal agency, despite their efforts contacting ICE and DHS to find out where he was. (Source)
The administration admitted that they did not have a warrant when they arrested Columbia University student Mahmoud Khalil. (Source)
The Trump administration continues to ignore and obstruct judge’s orders to provide information concerning the illegal removal of Kilmar Abrego Garcia. (Source 1, Source 2)
Garcia’s family was moved to a safe house after government court filings unnecessarily revealed their address. (Source)
A Trump-appointed judge ruled that the Trump administration needs to make an effort to return another man from the El Salvadoran prison back to the United States because he was sent there in violation of prior orders. (Source)
Though President Trump has now said that he won’t fire Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell (who Trump appointed in his first term), he still is setting up the incorrect claim that he has the power to do so. And Trump is capable of changing his mind at any time, as seen by the tariff roller coaster. (Source)
The nominee for IRS commissioner had a debt from his 2022 Senate campaign paid by campaign contributions from several companies that have been accused of participating in fraudulent tax credit schemes. The campaign debt was also a loan from the nominee himself, so paying off the debt amounted to paying the nominee directly. (Source)
A crypto entrepreneur who has spent $75 million on Trump crypto ventures had his charges from the Securities and Exchange Commission dropped. (Source)
Donald Trump is explicitly selling access to the White House by way of purchasing his “meme coin.” Top holders of the coin will get to attend a gala dinner with the President. It’s not even a campaign donation, but instead a payment directly into the pockets of the Trump family. (Source)
The Trump administration has attacked several universities, coercing them to change policies in order to keep federal funding. Donald Trump himself has also said that Harvard should lose its tax-exempt status, which would open a can of worms for any President to do so for any tax-exempt organizations with which they disagree.
The free speech organization FIRE (which represents groups and individuals across the political spectrum) has described the administration’s demands of universities as unconstitutional and “bullying [that] is so extreme it might more accurately be called extortion.” (Source 1, Source 2)
Under pressure from a federal investigation, the University of Tulane is investigating seven students for participation in an off-campus, peaceful protest. The students were not arrested or charged with crimes, but are being investigated because the group that organized the protest is “not in good standing with the university.” (Source 1, Source 2)
A whistleblower submitted a disclosure to Congress describing actions of DOGE at the National Labor Relations Board and concerns with data exiting the system. DOGE employees demanded access above typical admin levels, access that would allow unrestricted access to read and modify all data in the system, also demanding that the access not have the typical logging requirements that other accounts have. NLRB employees noticed that there was a huge spike in outgoing data from the agency’s systems. They also noted that almost immediately after DOGE employees were given access, a Russian IP address started attempting to log in with correct login information (the log-ins were blocked due to system protections).
When the whistleblower raised the concerns through internal channels, a couple of days later he found an envelope taped to his door with threats, personal information, and pictures of him walking his dog. (Source)
DOGE attempted to assign employees to the Vera Institute of Justice and other non-profits that have received funds from the federal government, but otherwise are not beholden to the government’s authority. (Source)

title: CLAUDE.md
text:
This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.


This is a Quarto blog (matthew_voss) — a static website built with Quarto and rendered to HTML. The blog contains political commentary posts by Matthew Voss. It is configured as an R project (mjv_blog.Rproj) but posts are plain Markdown (.qmd files) with no R code execution.



# Render the entire site
quarto render

# Preview the site locally with live reload
quarto preview

# Render a single post
quarto render posts/<post-folder>/index.qmd
The rendered output goes to docs/ (configured in _quarto.yml as output-dir: docs), which is what GitHub Pages serves. The _site/ directory is a legacy/mirror copy.




_quarto.yml — Site-level config: theme (cosmo + brand), output dir (docs/), navbar settings
posts/ — All blog posts, each in its own dated subfolder (e.g., posts/20251026/index.qmd)
posts/_metadata.yml — Applied to all posts: freeze: true (no code re-execution), banner-style title blocks
templates/index.qmd — Template for new posts
docs/ — Rendered site output (committed to git for GitHub Pages)
styles.css — Custom CSS overrides




Each post lives in posts/<YYYYMMDD>/index.qmd with this YAML front matter:
---
title: "Post Title"
author: "Matthew Voss"
date: "YYYY-MM-DD"
categories: [Authoritarianism, Corruption, Immigration]
editor:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

wrap: sentence — Markdown is wrapped at sentence boundaries (not word-wrapped)
Categories used: Authoritarianism, Corruption, Immigration (and others)
Posts use standard Markdown headers (##, ####) to organize topics
External citations are inline links: ([Source](URL))
freeze: true is set globally — computational output is frozen and never re-run




The docs/ directory is committed to git and served via GitHub Pages from the master branch. After rendering, commit the updated docs/ contents along with any new/changed .qmd files.

title: Facebook: April 2nd
text:
The following text is from a Facebook post made on April 2nd, 2025. (Original Post)
It’s time for me to make my first post in quite a while, to talk about the authoritarian direction of the Trump administration.
In the first two and a half months of this term, there have been many actions taken by the administration that I consider frightening. I have many policy disagreements and competency concerns as well, but moves towards authoritarianism are far more scary to me. Over the past few weeks I’ve been collecting many of these examples, which I’ll share here.
I’m sure I have many Facebook friends who will disagree with these perspectives or may not have heard of these stories. I encourage all to read them and really consider if you voted these kinds of actions, or whether a president that received a whopping 49.8% of the popular vote really has the mandate that he thinks he has to run roughshod over all other branches of government.
First off, the President said this weekend that he is “not joking” about pursuing a third term, going against the Constitution and tradition, as well as falsely claiming that he has high approval numbers that indicate that he should do so. (Source)
The administration has deported over 100 Venezuelans to an El Salvador prison without due process, accusing them of membership in the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua (TdA). Due process is important, because otherwise these individuals have no recourse to provide evidence of citizenship, legal status, and/or non-membership in said gang. At every turn, the administration has tried to block court orders to give some amount of due process (as required by the 5th and 14th Amendments).

“Border Czar” Tom Homan said “I don’t care what the judges think” in response to court orders. (Source)
President Trump called for impeachment of the judge who attempted to pause the deportations, a judge who was first appointed at the federal level under George W. Bush, and then elevated to district court in 2011 and confirmed unanimously by the Senate. (Source)
When the administration did finally provide limited evidence to another judge for these removals, she described the submission as “a terrible, terrible affidavit. If this were before me in a criminal case and you were asking to get a warrant issued on this, I’d throw you out of my chambers.” (Source)
This week, the administration admitted at least one individual was sent to El Salvador in error, but claims that it has no ability to bring him back to the United States.

This error from lack of due process shows that anyone–including citizens and legal non-citizens–could be deported with zero recourse. (Source)
Much of the evidence given thus far for those in that group of accused gang members is based on tattoos.
A Venezuelan journalist has said that “Tattoos aren’t an identifier for Tren de Araugua” and that instead many of these tattoos are popular among Latin American youth more generally. (Source)
Some of these individuals and tattoos include:

A soccer player with a Real Madrid tattoo (Source)
A makeup artist with tattoos of crowns for his mom and dad (Source)
Others with tattoos of hands, the words “family” and “brothers,” a ribbon representing the autism acceptance movement, and the name of a popular Puerto Rican pop album. (Source)

According to a court filing, even the Michael Jordan “Jump Man” logo is supposedly an indicator of TdA involvement, even though people around the world who have never even heard of the gang may have that exact same tattoo, or something very similar. (Page 14)
There are many other examples of lack of due process, cruel treatment, and detainment or deportation of previously legal residents without any kind of notice.
Earlier in March, a German national with a green card (a legal U.S. resident) was detained upon arriving in the U.S., stripped, and put in a cold shower. (Source)
A student was pulled directly off the street by masked officers, only finding out in that moment that her visa had been revoked. She was taken across the U.S., despite a court order that she remain in Massachusetts. She has not been accused of or charged with any crime. The only apparent explanation so far of her removal is an op-ed that offered criticism of her university. (Source)
A Canadian woman was held for two weeks, first detained while at an appointment to fix hang-ups with her visa application. She was willing to pay for her own flight back to Canada, but instead was shuttled around various detention centers that weren’t prepared to handle the influx of detainees. (Source)
A Cedar Rapids couple showed up for their check-in with ICE, and one of them was instead detained. (Source)
Numerous other examples of legal residents being deported or detained without notice (Source)
Beyond deportations, DOGE and Elon Musk have too many overreaches to count, all while typically lying about or at least misrepresenting the amount of fraud they have found. I’m happy to share more examples, but I’ll just share one DOGE-adjacent example from a niche area.
A couple of weeks ago, the Trump administration disbanded several volunteer advisory committees for the federal government’s statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, and the Census Bureau. These committees included data users from the private sector, academia, and non-profits. Federal data touches far more areas of society than many people realize, and it is vital to have trustworthy, unbiased data for decision-making. (Source)
Given that these committees were unpaid and their advice was non-binding, there was zero reason to disband them besides for wanting less oversight as data becomes more shoddy with layoffs or, dare I say, as the data is influenced by the politics at the top of the administration.
President Trump has also targeted law firms that have represented opponents of Trump in the past, by signing executive orders that could revoke security clearances or ban them from federal buildings. The President has made deals with several firms–or some might say bribes–with the firms promising pro bono work that will support policies aligned with President Trump’s in exchange for President Trump withdrawing the executive orders. (Source)
Finally, the President has pardoned or given significant deals to quite a few white-collar criminals who have aligned themselves with Trump.

A pardon for Trump donor Trevor Milton, who defrauded investors (Source)
Dropping charges against New York City mayor Eric Adams, in exchange for support for the President’s deportations (Source)
A pardon for corrupt former Illinois governor Rod Blagojevich (Source)
Pardons for the founders of BitMEX, a cryptocurrency exchange, who had failed to establish an anti-money laundering program for their exchange (Source)
The admin has dropped it’s case against a cryptocurrency firm who’s CEO donated $5 million to Trump’s inaugural committee (Source)
The DOJ dropped a case against Elon Musk’s firm SpaceX (Source)

If you’ve reached the end of this post, thank you! If all or any of these actions concern you, as they do me, I encourage you to express those concerns to your Senators and Representatives and consider how else you might be able to make your concerns known.

title: Facebook: August 1st
text:
The following text is from a Facebook post made on August 1st, 2025. (Original Post)
Today, President Trump fired the Commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics due to a jobs report published this morning that indicated a worsening economy. He claimed political manipulation of the data, while offering no factual evidence.
The previous BLS Commissioner, William Beach (appointed by Trump in his first term), described the firing in this way: “The totally groundless firing of Dr. Erika McEntarfer, my successor as Commissioner of Labor Statistics at BLS, sets a dangerous precedent and undermines the statistical mission of the Bureau.”
I’m biased due to my love of data, but I believe the production of reliable, objective data is one of the most important and useful functions of government agencies. However, from this point forward, every employee in one of those roles will work under the knowledge that they may get fired if the objective data they produce is unfavorable to the administration. That doesn’t sound like a constitutional republic to me.
Story on the firing of Dr. McEntarfer
Statement by former Commissioner Beach
Full statement by former Commissioner Beach and other experts in government data
Follow-up:
The President’s “evidence” is that the BLS published positive numbers for the Biden administration right before the election and revised them downwards by ~800,000 jobs after the election. This would not be hard evidence, but also is completely wrong, as the revision that Trump is referring to happened in August, long before the election. The jobs data published right before the election was actually very poor.
President Trump’s claims
August 2024 downward revision
October 2024 jobs report–published on 11/1, days before the election

title: Transparency and Truth
text:
There’s a lot going on right now that scares me, and the list below is just a small piece of it. But what might scare me the most is the short-term memory of those that justify them. Not long ago, anyone who would have predicted actions like these would have been accused of having Trump Derangement Syndrome. The line of what is acceptable gets pushed further and further. Now, it is just accepted that our President says so many things that are provably false (and often not even within the realm of possibility) or that he reposts AI-generated videos on his social media platform that feature him flying a fighter jet and dropping poop on those who protest him.
My question for all Donald Trump supporters is simply: Where is the line and how will you respond when he crosses it?

title: Transparency and Truth
text:
The Pentagon

Transparency and the Press
Members of the Trump administration have often described themselves or President Trump as the most transparent [insert agency here] in history. In practice, that hasn’t really been the case.
For the Department of Defense (Congress has not yet changed the name to the Department of War), there has been a lot of coverage of their modified press policy. Almost all of the previous news agencies covering the Pentagon chose to not to sign the new policy, including conservative news outlets like Fox News and Newsmax. Right-wing personalities and administration officials have claimed that this is because the department tightened up rules on where press could go in the Pentagon. However, those claims ignore the additional policies that threaten the press for reporting on news that has not been approved by Pentagon officials–an important part of the job of the press to maintain accountability when a department is not transparent, no matter how much they claim they are. (Source)
In the last week, the Pentagon announced the new press corps that will be reporting from the Pentagon. (Source) This group is filled with the most extreme organizations, ones that go beyond having any kind of ideological lean, but are blatant advocacy groups for Donald Trump. With that in mind, the Pentagon should not be “announcing” any kind of press corps, because the press corps should not representing the public, not the administration.


Illegal Killings
While the Pentagon has been working to get a more accomodating press corps, they have been giving essentially zero information on strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific on what they claim to be drug smugglers, killing more than 40 people so far. The administration claims that it has the legal authority to do so, but has given little detail on what that authority is, both to the public and to Congress. (Source) Previous administrations would give briefings to Congress on significant foreign strikes, but the Trump administration has opted to not even do that. Republican Senator Rand Paul has described the strikes as “extrajudicial killings” and has emphasized that zero evidence has been given, even to Congress, on why strikes were necessary or justified in these situations. (Source)
Note: On Wednesday, the administration finally gave a briefing, but only to Senate Republicans. On Thursday, the administration gave a briefing to the full House Armed Services Committee, but the briefing did not offer reasoning for why lethal force was necessary. (Source)
Some might argue that killing someone smuggling drugs is a reasonable action. I would argue it is not, especially considering that if the U.S. government can track the boat in order to strike it with a missile, they are also likely capable of capturing the individuals. It is applying the death penalty without having to provide evidence or prove the case in front of a court. In the one case where the U.S. did capture two individuals who survived a strike, the administration chose to release them from U.S. custody back into South America, bringing questions of why it is necessary to kill the accused, but not hold them for investigation and prosecution. (Source) A couple of weeks ago, the U.S. Navy commander overseeing the strikes stepped down. There have not been reports on why, but the timing certainly brings questions of his views of the legality of the strikes. (Source)


Corruption
The Department of Defense awarded a contract to a drone company that has given Donald Trump Jr. an ownership stake in exchange for his role as an advisor. Donald Trump Jr. helped screen candidates for jobs at the Pentagon and has said that he promoted candidates who supported expanding drone usage. (Source)

title: Transparency and Truth
text:
White House East Wing & Ballroom
President Trump has chosen to tear down the East Wing of the White House–which mainly contained offices for the first lady and her staff and some other executive offices. In it’s place, the president intends to build a 90,000 sq. ft. ballroom that will dwarf the other parts of the White House (the main, Executive Residence, portion of the White House is only 55,000 sq. ft. Source). It’s not the craziest idea to me–it makes sense that the White House should have a larger space for entertaining and state dinners than it currently has. However, doing all of this in a short time span, without approval from Congress, at least feels wrong. And soliciting private donations that amount to hundreds of millions of dollars for a pet project of the president continues to escalate the transactional nature of the Trump administration.
Donald Trump loves naming things after himself. You only have to look at all of his business enterprises to see that. Upon reports that he planned on naming the ballroom after himself, he denied it. However, even on the list of donors for the ballroom provided by the White House itself, the ballroom was already referred to as the President Donald J. Trump Ballroom. (Source). A leader naming things after himself reminds you more of Russia, North Korea, or other dictatorships, but I suppose it shouldn’t be too surprising when President Trump has also hung huge banners of his face on federal buildings (Source).

title: Transparency and Truth
text:
Elections
Former Trump aide Steve Bannon said that Donald Trump will run for president again in 2028, and that there is a plan to make that happen. Trump himself has at times said that of course he wouldn’t, but has also mused about it to reporters, encouraged his supporters when they say it, and sells “Trump 2028” hats in the Trump Organization store. (Source)
The Trump administration will be sending election monitors to California and New Jersey for their fall elections. These elections are not federal elections–they will not have any races for the U.S. House or Senate. The Department of Justice has not provided an explanation of why these elections deserve monitoring, just that they have received requests to do so from Republicans in the states. This is the first action of the Trump administration directly meddling with state-run elections. (Source)
At the same time, the Trump administration has filled important election security roles with proponents of 2020 election conspiracies. One of these officials suggested in March, before her appointment, that a national emergency declaration could be used by the administration to dictate election rules to state and local governments. (Source)
In regards to the 2020 election, it’s always worth a reminder that Donald Trump lost nearly every court case where he claimed fraud or any issues with the election. (Source) In Republican-run investigations after the election, no hard evidence was ever provided that indicates substantial election fraud.

title: Transparency and Truth
text:
Pardons
This week, President Trump added to his list of pardons by granting one to the founder and majority owner of Binance, a large cryptocurrency exchange that also happened to recently make a deal with World Liberty Financial, which is the Trump family cryptocurrency firm that has made hundreds of millions of dollars for Donald Trump and his family. Changpeng Zhao, the individual who was pardoned, had pled guilty to enabling money laundering, as Binance had enabled transactions by groups such as al-Qaida, Hamas, and ISIS. (Source)
President Trump also commuted the sentence George Santos, the disgraced former Congressman who pled guilty to wire fraud and identity theft. Santos had been kicked out of Congress on a significant bipartisan vote after lying about large portions of his resume and on campaign finance reports. (Source)
These actions add to the list of President Trump’s pardons and commutations for political allies, regardless of their crimes. The list includes significant donors, others tied to cryptocurrency and other industries favored by Trump, and politicians elected from either party who have since declared themselves Trump supporters. Not to mention the 1,500+ pardons and commutations for those involved in the January 6th storming of the Capitol, one of whom was recently re-arrested for threats made against Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries, as well as at least 10 others who have been re-arrested for other crimes such has child sexual abuse and plots to murder FBI agents. (Source)

title: Corporate Murder, Corruption, and Continued Cruelty
text:
Just before the war in Iran, the Department of Defense declared Anthropic, the company that makes the Claude AI chatbot, a “supply-chain risk” over a contract dispute. The contract dispute was over a contract that the DOD had already agreed to(!!) and Anthropic simply refused to modify the terms. Obviously it would be well within reason for the department to choose to not renew the contract if they did not like the terms, but they took it a step further, trying to force Anthropic to accept the modifications by threatening the supply-chain risk designation. This designation has never been applied to a domestic company; it is typically reserved for companies in foreign adversary countries. The designation would mean that Anthropic could not do any business with another federal contractor, which would include every other large technology company and some of Anthropic’s largest investors. Anthropic already won a preliminary injunction in court, but the case will go continue on.
Dean Ball served as an advisor for the Trump administration’s AI Action Plan, released last summer. He accurately described the Trump administration’s action as an “intention to commit corporate murder.” (Source) In a Tweet, he went on to describe the action as a “psychotic power grab” and a claim that “the DoD can force all contractors to stop doing business of any kind with arbitrary other companies.” (Source)
The Trump administration has taken other significant actions to grab power in private companies in a way that is unprecedented. However, this is a step even further, with the administration demanding that a private company do business with the government, or else it will effectively be shut down. It’s laughable for an administration theoretically representing the party of small government, and a party that would relentlessly criticize such actions from a Democratic administration, or a disfavored foreign nation.

title: Corporate Murder, Corruption, and Continued Cruelty
text:
Corruption
The Trump administration continues to provide financial benefits for political allies and Trump family members.
The Cato Institute, which is not a leftist organization, has analyzed what it describes as a “blizzard” of second-term pardons, noting that over $1.5 billion in criminal debt has been forgiven for political allies and donors. During the Biden administration, his pardons forgave a bit under $700,000. $700,000 may also sound like a lot, but it is 0.05% of the amount that has already been forgiven in one year of the Trump administration. (Source)
With actions in the war in Iran, there have been several instances of actions that may indicate insider trading by those with knowledge of Trump administration actions. At the beginning of the war, a Polymarket trader placed several suspiciously well-timed bets on actions related to the attacks on Iran. These bets made the trader over $500,000. Notably, the Trump family has significant ties to Polymarket, and the administration has dropped two investigations into Polymarket. (Source) A few weeks later, there was a very large amount of movement, over half a billion dollars in contracts, in the oil futures market just about 10 minutes before President Trump announced that the United States and Iran were in talks for “COMPLETE AND TOTAL RESOLUTION OF OUR HOSTILITIES IN THE MIDDLE EAST.” That announcement has obviously not yet borne out, but it appears that someone had significant financial benefits from the announcement. The Trump administration’s Commodity Futures Trading Commission does not yet appear to be interested in investigating these incidents. (Source)
Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, serves as a negotiator in the MIddle East for the Trump administration. At the same time, he is raising money for his private equity firm from the very same governments with which he is negotiating. He has reportedly seeked to raise over $5 billion from these governments or groups closely tied with them. Since the administration has not made him an official government employee, he is not required to report conflicts of interest. (Source)

title: Corporate Murder, Corruption, and Continued Cruelty
text:
Courts vs. The Administration
The relationship between the federal judiciary and the Trump administration has continued to deteriorate. Judges have expressed serious frustration with the Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security for violating court orders and appearing unprepared for cases. Judges appointed by presidents of both parties, including Trump-appointed judges, have ruled against the administration’s mass detention policy with an overwhelming majority. (Source)
In Minnesota, Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz warned of criminal contempt charges after finding the government had violated more than 200 court orders in his district alone — a level of defiance he called historic. (Source)
Nationally, there have been at least 35 instances since August where judges have demanded that the administration explain why it should not be punished for violating court orders. (Source)
A judge in New Jersey ruled that federal prosecutors have lost their credibility by “intentionally” ignoring judicial mandates. (Source)
The Justice Department itself acknowledged violating more than 50 court orders in New Jersey, offering “sky-high caseloads” as the explanation for illegal deportations and missed deadlines. (Source)

title: Corporate Murder, Corruption, and Continued Cruelty
text:
ICE Enforcement: “Unimaginable Cruelty”
The administration has consistently claimed it is focused on dangerous criminals. The data tells a different story. And cruelty continues in the treatment of those detainees who have no criminal record, from releasing detainees in the cold without their personal items or any way to contact anyone for assistance, to failures to provide medical care inside detention centers and reported betting pools about suicidal detainees.
Nearly 75% of ICE detainees have no criminal conviction, according to ICE’s own data. (Source)
One Trump-appointed judge harshly criticized Department of Homeland Security treatment of a man with no criminal record, who entered the U.S. at age 9. He described the treatment as “unimaginable cruelty” and said, “the laws of human decency condemn such villainy.” (Source)
A different Trump-appointed judge found that ICE and CBP have adopted policies authorizing investigatory stops based solely on race or ethnicity — not on any individualized suspicion of wrongdoing. (Source)
A Wall Street Journal investigation found that the majority of people accused of “assaulting” agents during immigration operations are U.S. citizens. Out of the 181 U.S. citizens accused on social media, none of them have been convicted at trial, and video evidence has frequently contradicted the government’s version of events. A majority of those U.S. citizens haven’t even had charges pressed, despite the department already charging and convicting them on social media. (Source)
There have also been significant failures in basic due process. A federal judge ordered the administration to bring back a man who was deported to Mexico in violation of a court-issued stay, noting that he was likely denied access to legal counsel and proper translation services. (Source)
In a separate case, ICE labeled a man “the worst of the worst” and held him for six weeks, despite ending up dropping his charges. The judge ordered his release. (Source)
In St. Paul, a contempt hearing was held because ICE failed to return the IDs, phones, and cash of 28 immigrants who were released into the cold without even warm clothing. (Source)
Another judge ordered ICE to return essential personal property, such as work authorizations and licenses, to six detainees or face further contempt charges. (Source)
Reports have also surfaced about deteriorating conditions inside ICE detention centers, where many migrants are held for over six months despite being willing to accept deportation, and where a string of suicides has drawn attention to a facility in Texas. (Source) (Source)

Judge Tostrud found that ICE and CBP have adopted policies authorizing investigatory stops based solely on race or ethnicity — not on any individualized suspicion of wrongdoing. (Source) That is not immigration enforcement. That is racial profiling enshrined in policy.

(Source) In a separate case, ICE labeled a man “the worst of the worst” and held him for six weeks without charges — a judge threatened contempt and ordered his release. (Source) In St. Paul, a contempt hearing was held because ICE failed to return the IDs, phones, and cash of 28 immigrants who were released into the cold without even warm clothing. (Source) Judge Tunheim subsequently ordered ICE to return essential personal property — including work authorizations and licenses — to six detainees or face further contempt charges. (Source)
Reports have also surfaced about deteriorating conditions inside ICE detention centers, where many migrants are held for over six months despite being willing to accept deportation, and where a string of suicides has drawn attention to a facility in Texas. (Source) (Source)
The administration often says these individuals should have come here legally. That argument has nothing to do with whether the government gets to detain someone for six weeks without charges, deport someone in defiance of a court order, or seize personal property and simply not return it. Those are not immigration policy questions. Those are basic legal and human rights questions.

Pardons
The Cato Institute — not a left-leaning organization — has analyzed what it describes as a “blizzard” of second-term pardons, noting that over $1.5 billion in criminal debt has been forgiven for political allies and donors. (Source) For context, previous administrations wiped out far smaller sums through clemency. (Source) The traditional vetting process for pardons has been bypassed entirely.
This continues a trend I have written about before. The pardon power is being used not to correct injustices in the legal system, but to reward loyalty and erase consequences for those in the president’s orbit.

section: The Pentagon and Conflicts of Interest
text:
The Pentagon and Conflicts of Interest
ProPublica has investigated a “web of financial ties” involving Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg and other officials who retain links to the industries they now regulate. (Source) This is exactly the kind of structural corruption that should draw bipartisan concern. When the people making decisions about defense contracts have personal financial stakes in the outcomes, the public interest is not being served.

title: Courts, Contempt, and Cruelty
section: A Note on AI and the Military
text:
A Note on AI and the Military
One story worth watching: there is an escalating conflict between the Department of Defense and Anthropic — the company that makes the Claude AI model — over usage restrictions that Anthropic has placed on its product in military contexts. (Source) Secretary Hegseth has threatened to designate Anthropic as a supply-chain risk over the dispute. (Source)
I am not taking a position here on what rules AI companies should or shouldn’t impose. But the idea that a company declining to remove its own safety restrictions from a product it built could be designated a national security threat is deeply troubling. It suggests the administration believes it can coerce private companies into removing guardrails by threatening them with government blacklisting. That is not how a free market is supposed to work.
